_comment: Shared FAAB baseline-bid parity fixture. SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for both tests/trade/test_faab_bid_parity.py (drives src/trade/waiver.py::_compute_faab_bid) and frontend/__tests__/faab-bid-parity.test.js (drives frontend/lib/waiver-logic.js::computeFaabHint). Neither test may hardcode an expectation of its own — if the two implementations disagree, exactly one of them fails against this file. Every `expected` below is hand-derived from the formula in `rounding`, not produced by running either implementation.
generatedFor: sitewide math audit finding H4 (server bid vs client hint disagreed by $1 at every .5 boundary)

formula.guard: candidateValue <= 0 or budget <= 0 -> (0, 0, 0), no dollar floor

rounding.why: Python's round() is half-to-even and JS's Math.round is half-up, so a shared formula that leans on either default splits at .5. Half-up is chosen because it is the money convention users expect ($10.50 bids $11) and it is what the client hint already displayed.
rounding.alsoNote: reasonable/lowball scale the UNROUNDED aggressive figure. Scaling the rounded one made them percentages of a rounded number (70% of $18 instead of 70% of $17.50).

cases.why: share 1.0 -> 30% of $100 = $30. Lowball is exactly $10.50 — the boundary where banker's rounding said $10 and half-up says $11.
share 0.5 -> 17.5% of $100 = $17.50 -> $18. Reasonable is 70% of 17.50 = 12.25 -> $12; scaling the rounded $18 would have said $13.
30% of $50 = $15. Reasonable is exactly $10.50 -> $11 under half-up.
17.5% of $200 = $35. Reasonable is exactly $24.50 -> $25 (banker's rounds to the even $24).
A null pool top means the candidate IS the top: share 1.0, same as the first case.
share is clamped by max(candidate, top), so a candidate richer than the stated top still tops out at 1.0.
$1 budget x 5.0025% = $0.05. Every tier floors at $1 rather than rounding down to a $0 bid.
H4: a manager with $0 remaining cannot bid. Zero is NOT a missing budget — it must not fall back to a full $100.
Sleeper can report an over-spent roster as negative; same answer as zero, and the $1 floor does not apply.
A non-positive player value short-circuits before the dollar floor.
